title: Developmental disability program faces serious challenges; stakeholders must be included in answers
summary: “Nothing about us, without us!” The Maryland Department of Health appears to have forgotten that rallying cry when it presented rules changes for the Developmental Disabilities Administration, but it can and should, writes Rachel London.
content:
by Rachel London, Maryland Matters December 6, 2024

by Rachel London, Maryland Matters December 6, 2024

“Nothing about us, without us!”

It’s not just a slogan. It’s a call to action, that no policy should be decided without the direct participation from the people affected by that policy.

The Nov. 22 article about the Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA) rule changes shows the frustration of people with disabilities, families and the Department of Health as everyone navigates the changes.

The article also reveals what is missing: The Department did not proactively engage with stakeholders, including the people who are most impacted by these changes. But they can and should.

There are many Marylanders who need supports from DDA. In fact, over 18,000 people with developmental disabilities rely on services through the DDA Medicaid waivers. They can choose to receive those services and supports in two ways – by self-directing their services or from one of the hundreds of community providers licensed by DDA. All of the vital supports help make sure people with disabilities get to live, work, and thrive in our communities.

We at the Developmental Disabilities Coalition are a group of five statewide organizations that work together to create change so people with developmental disabilities and their families have access to services and supports provided by an effective system that is responsive to their needs. With more than two decades of experience as people with disabilities, families, providers, professionals and advocates, we are fully committed to, “Nothing about us, without us!”

We understand there are serious challenges: This administration inherited structural challenges and Maryland is facing a budget crisis. We are partners of DDA and we want change.

But change must follow DDA’s mission of “person-centered, family-oriented” and include community involvement, adequate communication and sufficient funding. And any policy change must always meet the full array of needs of people eligible for DDA services and support, and in the model of people’s choosing – whether that be the Community Provider Model or Self-Directed Services Model.

The DD Coalition appreciates the department’s intention with the policy change is for more clarity, consistency and fairness in the self-directed services model. However, intention is different from impact, and the new policy creates confusion and challenges for many people.

While Secretary Laura Herrera Scott states there are opportunities for public involvement, like monthly meetings, no such public meetings are posted on the website. Further, it remains unclear how to provide official feedback and whether it will be considered.

Any proposed changes in policies that support this community should include the full, direct, consistent and transparent participation of this community so there is meaningful inclusion of their opinions and consideration of unintended consequences. Nothing about us without us!
